<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Joe Courtney, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark Takano, Rep. Alma S. Adams, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Donald Norcross, Rep. Lucy McBath, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Rep. Haley M. Stevens, Rep. Greg Casar, Rep. Summer L. Lee, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Yassamin Ansari>: Introduction
H.R. 4054, the Accreditation Choice and Innovation Act, makes sweeping reforms to the higher education accreditation process. In general, these ill-informed reforms will create loopholes in the oversight of both institutions and accreditors which will in turn establish untested pathways to federal funding, insert politics and culture wars into the accreditation process, and erode the quality of higher education. H.R. 4054 builds on the harmful policies proposed by both the first and current Trump Administration to further this Administration's attack on American higher education.
H.R. 4054 IS PART OF THE REPUBLICAN PATTERN OF WEAPONIZING HIGHER
EDUCATION ACCREDITATION
During the first Trump Administration, Department of Education (Department) Secretary Betsy DeVos drastically shook up the college accreditation process by dismantling the regional accreditation framework and allowing colleges to ``accreditor-hop'' to new agencies.\1\ The current Trump Administration has continued efforts to weaken higher education accreditation. On April 28, President Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14279, Reforming Accreditation to Strengthen Higher Education, which directs the Secretary of Education (Secretary) to hold accreditors accountable for what he deemed as ``unlawful'' Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) actions and litmus tests to ``realign'' accreditation with other standards seemingly tailored towards student achievement.\2\ This EO unfairly targets accreditors for the actions of their accredited colleges that the President deems incongruous with his vision for higher education. While accreditors do examine college DEI policies as part of their assessment, that examination is largely focused on determining whether colleges are living up to what they themselves are claiming they are doing. The EO also establishes a process to make it easier for colleges to change accreditors to evade sufficient oversight, which will undermine the primary purpose of accreditation: to ensure students attend high-quality, well-governed institutions. The Council of Regional Accrediting Commissions, which represents all institutional accrediting agencies, ``firmly reject[s] President Trump's mischaracterization of accreditor's role'' in the EO and other remarks.\3\
\1\Paul Fain, New Rules on Accreditation and State Authorization, Inside Higher Ed (Octo. 31, 2019), https://www.insidehighered.com/news/ 2019/11/01/education-department-issues-new-regulations-accreditation-and-state-authorization.
\2\Exec. Order No. 14279, 90 Fed. Reg. 17529 (Apr. 23, 2025).
\3\Press Release, Council of Reg. Accred. Commissions, Accreditors React to President Trump's Latest Executive Order Targeting College Oversight (Apr. 23, 2025), https://www.c-rac.org/post/accreditors-react-to-president-trump-s-latest-executive-order-targeting-college-oversight.
Congressional Republicans have a very similar vision for accreditation to the President's, pushing to open the doors to new, untested accreditors, politicize accreditation, and make it easier for both colleges and accreditors to evade accountability. In the 118th Congress, the Committee and House considered several bills that would further weaponize the accreditation system to weed out practices that Republicans dislike.\4\ Committee Democrats know the accreditation process can and should be reformed. However, it is essential that such reforms protect the role and independence of accrediting agencies and not attack them for doing what the federal government has designated them to do: oversee institutional quality.
\4\Press Release, Cmte. on Educ. & Workforce Democrats, While You Were Sleeping, Extreme Republicans Voted to Raise College Costs, Return to DeVos Era Deregulation and Chaos (Jan. 31, 2024), https://democrats-edworkforce.house.gov/media/press-releases/while-you-were-sleeping-extreme-republicans-voted-to-raise-college-costs-return-to-devos-era-deregulation-and-chaos; Press Release, Cmte. on Educ. & Workforce Democrats, Committee Republicans Vote to Weaken Worker Protections, Fuel Culture Wars, and Undermine Public Education (Mar. 21, 2024), https://democrats-edworkforce.house.gov/media/press-releases/committee-republicans-vote-to-weaken-worker-protections-fuel-culture-wars-and-undermine-public-education.
H.R. 4054 CREATES UNTESTED PATHWAYS TO FEDERAL RECOGNITION AND ERODES
OVERSIGHT OF COLLEGES AND ACCREDITORS
H.R. 4054 establishes several alarming untested pathways to recognition for prospective accreditors and new paths for low-quality education providers to receive Title IV aid by circumventing accreditor oversight. The legislation also erodes the federal government's ability to provide oversight of the accreditation process. H.R. 4054 represents an alarming shift away from the traditional higher education ``triad'' framework ensuring program integrity (with separate roles for the federal government, states, and accrediting agencies) to a framework that fundamentally threatens oversight of program quality and consumer protection.\5\
\5\Wesley Whistle, Outsourcing Accreditor Oversight to States: A bad Idea in the Making: Why Letting States Approve Accreditors Puts Students and Taxpayers at Risk, New America (Jun. 25, 2025), https:// www.newamerica.org/education-policy/edcentral/outsourcing-accreditor-oversight-to-states-a-bad-idea-in-the-making/.
Accelerated Path to Recognition for Accreditors
Section 2(b) establishes an accelerated path to federal recognition for untested accreditors at both the program-level and institution-level of accreditation. Under current laws and regulations, in order to receive federal recognition, the credential that empowers an accreditor to determine whether a program or institution can receive federal student aid, an accreditor must typically provide the Department with proof of two years of experience it has in accrediting institutions.\6\ H.R. 4054 would circumvent this requirement, allowing untested prospective accreditors to gain federal recognition without adequately proving their ability to oversee colleges, which prevents the Department from ensuring quality institutional accreditation. Recognizing untested accreditors will likely result in lower quality oversight of accreditation at the institutional level. By providing underperforming institutions with a loophole to accreditation and federal student aid eligibility while evading accountability, H.R. 4050 will weaking the current higher ed oversight triad.\7\
\6\34 C.F.R. Sec. 602.12(a)(2) (2025)(An agency seeking initial recognition must demonstrate that it has . . . [c]onducted accrediting activities, including deciding whether to grant or deny accreditation or preaccreditation, for at least two years prior to seeking recognition . . .).
\7\Letter from Third Way to the U.S. Dep't. of Educ. Sec'y Miguel Cardona (Jan. 9, 2024), available at https://www.thirdway.org/letter/ letter-to-the-department-of-education-on-accreditation-rulemaking.
State Accreditors
Section 2(a)(3)(D) allows states to serve as an accreditor or to designate their own accrediting bodies to focus on specific workforce needs. The legislation provides a minimal process for secretarial approval (based entirely on state determinations) of these state-designated accrediting agencies. While this sounds viable in theory, we know many states do not have the capacity to serve as accreditors, given the meager resources they commit to their already-legislated role in the accountability triad as state authorizing agencies.\8\ This new provision could also create significant differences in how colleges are accredited in states that take their consumer protection role seriously, and those who take a more laissez-faire approach,\9\ especially should H.R. 4054 be enacted in conjunction with H.R. 2516, the Accreditation for College Excellence Act.\10\ H.R. 4054 would empower a state with a lax state authorization history to designate a similarly lax state accrediting entity, in effect collapsing two legs of the accountability triad in an effort to attract schools that could neither be authorized nor accredited elsewhere. Allowing states to serve as accrediting bodies also severely limits the Secretary's accreditation oversight responsibilities, which is concerning particularly because states have a well-documented history of avoiding federal oversight in student aid programs.\11\
\8\Whistle, supra note 5; David Tandberg et al., Improving State Authorization: The State Role in Ensuring Quality and Consumer Protection in Higher Education, State Higher Educ. Exec 18-19 (Jul. 2019), https://sheeo.org/improving-state-authorization-the-state-role-in-ensuring-quality-and-consumer-protection-in-higher-education/.
\9\Whistle, supra note 5.
\10\Accreditation for College Excellence Act, H.R. 2516, 119th Cong. (2024), https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/ 2516/text.
\11\Whistle, supra note 5.
Accreditor Shopping
Section 2(e) of H.R. 4054 allows any college or program to change its accrediting body without the approval of the Secretary. This builds off of EO14279 which directs the Department to ``streamline the process . . . to change accreditors.''\12\ Making a college's ability to change accreditors frictionless will undoubtedly harm students; by removing the requirement of the Secretary's approval, many colleges looking to evade oversight could do so simply by finding an accreditor with less rigorous standards. There is already a test case for what happens when colleges can easily switch accreditors: Florida. In 2022, Florida passed a law requiring all colleges to change their accreditor after every accreditation cycle.\13\ This has already resulted in chaos and backlogs at the Department as staff work to review these accreditor changes in a timely manner.\14\ In a world where predatory institutions are already testing the fence of effective oversight for weakness when it comes to accreditor shopping, H.R. 4054 cuts down the fence.
\12\Executive Order 14279 supra note 2.
\13\Gray Rohrer, Gov. DeSantis signs higher education bill with post-tenure review, accreditation changes, Florida Politics (Apr. 19, 2022), https://floridapolitics.com/archives/517541-gov-desantis-signs-higher-education-bill-with-post-tenure-review-accreditation-changes/.
\14\Josh Moody, Florida Officials Fume Over Sluggish Accreditation Changes, Inside Higher Educ. (Nov. 11, 2024), https:// www.insidehighered.com/news/governance/accreditation/2024/11/11/ florida-officials-fume-over-sluggish-accreditation-changes.
Substantive Changes Review
Under current law, when colleges want to make substantive changes--such as adding a new program offering, degree level, learning modality, or campus location--they are required to inform their accreditor.\15\ The accreditor is responsible for confirming that the college has the resources and ability to implement said substantive change. Section 2(c)(3) of H.R. 4054 drastically loosens the requirements for when an accreditor must review substantive changes. It requires accreditors to review colleges' substantive changes only if they significantly impact the college's mission, legal status, or ownership, create new programs at a higher credential level, or merge with another college. This was designed to reduce the review burden on accreditors; however, alleviating the burden creates a large loophole for colleges to evade oversight during key substantive changes, such as moving programs to online platforms. This change will allow poor-quality programs to not only thrive but expand.\16\
\15\Developing Substantive Change Proposals, WASC Senior College and University Commission, https://www.wscuc.org/resources/subchange-proposals (last accessed Sept. 13, 2025).
